trajectory.thought: The leader is a seeded baseline (median of full pool) and the verdict is 'indistinguishable' — the runner-up is not statistically better. Given the unstable ranking (Kendall tau -0.06), very high error correlation (0.944), and only 3 validation windows making weight estimation high-variance, the robust median of the full pool is the natural choice. More turns are unlikely to turn noise into a real gain here.

action_args.justification: The series is trend-dominated with weak seasonality and non-stationary. Model ranking is unstable across windows (Kendall tau -0.06) and error correlation is very high (mean 0.944, one large redundant group), so fitted weights would chase noise over only 3 validation windows. The median of the full pool is the most robust combination: it is insensitive to the few outlying models, does not depend on a stable ranking, and naturally down-weights the tail of the error distribution. The leader is a seed with an 'indistinguishable' margin over the runner-up, confirming no statistically better alternative exists in the tested set.

   - Only 3 independent groups
   - Relative spread is 0.251 (moderate)
   - Best models: ONLY_DWT_rf, DWT_rf, FT_catboost, DWT_catboost, CWT_catboost

3. **Attempt History**: All 10 attempts are baselines. The leader is "median" (full pool) with score 0.7094. The runner-up margin is 0.0192 and verdict is "indistinguishable."

Wait, let me re-read the stopping rule: "If the leader is a SEED and the verdict is 'indistinguishable', accept it. The runner-up is not statistically better and more turns rarely turn noise into a real gain."

The leader is "median" with origin "baseline" - that's a seed. The verdict is "indistinguishable." So according to the stopping rules, I should accept it.

The median is already the most robust simple combination. The error correlation is very high (0.944), meaning most models are essentially saying the same thing. The ranking is unstable.

- The stopping rule explicitly says to accept in this case
- The median of the full pool is already the most robust option
- High error correlation means pruning won't help much (most models are redundant)
- Unstable ranking means fitted weights are high-variance

I think the right call is to accept the leader. The median of the full pool is a robust, simple combination that handles the unstable ranking and correlated errors well. There's no clear hypothesis that would beat it given the series characteristics.
